speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, by the aggregate macro indicators, we grew slower, but we are not in recession.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Based on the Ministry of Trade and Industry's (MTI's) forecast for the year, we should not be in recession this year as well.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But is this the situation on the ground?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Based on sentiment surveys and many other anecdotal observations and feedback, businesses have reflected that times are bad and many are struggling to manage both top and bottom lines.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Are we at risk of entering into a recession?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is extending the decline of 6% in the preceding quarter.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Manufacturing, which includes electronics and the oil and gas sectors, tends to be more outward-oriented and, hence, are directly exposed to the current weak global demand.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The current narrative for the global growth outlook does not look good as well.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Just two days ago, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) warned of the loss of growth momentum and frigidity in the global economy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Since the start of the year, uncertainty and downside risks have also increased, the state of China's economy being the foremost concern.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If China dropped the ball on its reform to rebalance its economy, we could see a much sharper slowdown in its growth and it will hit us directly and immediately.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On the home front, we are pressing on with restructuring and industry transformation as laid out in the Industry Transformation Roadmap, pending the completion of the review.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Against these forces at play, what is MTI's latest view on the economy this year and whether our economy is resilient enough to cope with the external shocks and the internal restructuring?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Does MTI intend to do more to help companies manage the downside risks and uncertainties?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For this year's Committee of Supply (COS), would MTI introduce more support for companies, especially small and medium enterprises (SMEs) looking to expand overseas?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Their continued growth and vibrancy are of utmost importance to achieving our goal of becoming an innovative and value-creating economy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As we restructure the economy, we have to help our SMEs build capabilities, including improving productivity, and seek growth opportunities through internationalising.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The risks of SMEs being displaced as we restructure the economy are real.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While it is not possible to save any single company from failing, our economic agencies should do their utmost to help the SMEs transform, upgrade and capture new growth opportunities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But then, on the defensive, we should gear ourselves to ride on this wave of change and seize the new opportunities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Obviously, it will require us to reorientate and, more importantly, for the workers to reskill for the new types of jobs to come.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Lifelong learning and continuous skills upgrading are the best defence against skills obsolescence and structural unemployment.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But I believe that MTI and its agencies can also work with the industries and companies to leverage the resources offered by SkillsFuture and ensure the skills readiness of our workers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It will require greater horizontal coordination and management attention on the part of the stakeholders involved so that we can achieve the desired state of right jobs, right skills and right match, as articulated by the Minister for Finance yesterday.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In this era of fast-paced technological changes and never-ending innovation, it is increasingly challenging to predict product trends or to anticipate what the next big thing would be.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In that regard, the CFE has a very tough job.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: The Economic Development Board (EDB) was established in the 1960s to assist the newly independent Singapore to create jobs for Singaporeans by attracting foreign investments to our shores.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: All these years, EDB has done an excellent job, successfully attracting many multinational companies to Singapore and creating many jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: However, today's economic and job considerations for Singapore are very different from past decades.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Land is becoming scarcer and there is also a "social limit" in the number of foreign workers that Singapore can accommodate.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Robotics, automation and offshoring are also replacing workers in many sectors, including jobs held by professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMETs).

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: I would, therefore, like to ask the Minister how MTI and EDB will go about addressing such factors as I have described.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Most importantly, how would his Ministry seek out or attract companies and industries abroad which will best create jobs with skills requirement that matches what our Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) are producing and that are more resilient to automation and offshoring?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: If we can do this well, we can then attract the right companies to be based here to provide high-quality and more enduring jobs suited to our local conditions and also the skillsets that Singaporean workers either possess now or those skillsets that our IHLs are producing.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: The underlying principles of AEC are the free flow of goods, services, investments, capital and skilled labour.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Many Singapore businesses are excited about AEC as there will be lower barriers to trade and investments.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: AEC could also lead to the expansion of financial products and services in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) region and could benefit Singapore as ASEAN's regional financial hub.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Conversely, there are some views here in Singapore that our workers may not benefit as they will lose jobs as other ASEAN countries attract investments to their shores.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Workers here are also concerned about job losses as Singapore companies based here right now may relocate production or services to cheaper and more barrier-free ASEAN countries.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Would the Minister share his views on these common fears and whether or not they are valid?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: What can Singapore companies and workers do to minimise the negative implications of AEC and to capitalise on the benefits offered by AEC?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: I do take note at this point that free-trade agreements are not necessarily a zero-sum game, as Minister Vivian Balakrishnan has spoken about just now.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Third, Madam, is on the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP) agreement.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Representing Singapore in Auckland for the TPP signing was Minister Lim Hng Kiang himself, and the Minister had spoken about the benefits to Singapore investors and businesses of a more open, predictable and transparent regional marketplace.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: The leaders of the other TPP members also hailed the agreement, with US President Barack Obama saying that the TPP would give the US an advantage over other leading economies, naming China as one that the US would have advantage over, and it is a trade deal "that puts American workers first".

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: However, in contrast to that view, there are many anti-TPP protesters who blocked streets in Auckland, with protesters indicating their concerns that "the TPP is less about jobs and more about big businesses and corporate greed", to borrow their words, and highlighting fears that the TPP was weighted in the US' favour.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Yet, on the other hand, various US Presidential candidates have recently threatened not to recommend a ratification of the TPP by the US Congress.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: If anything, the views are, indeed, very varied and sometimes conflicting.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Is it true that the TPP is weighted in the US' favour and provides less benefits to other countries and Singapore?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: There are some, in our midst, who are worried that such free trade agreements may mean that Singapore will open its doors more freely to other professionals coming to Singapore to work.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Can the Minister clarify this issue, because I believe that these are quite of concern to many Singaporeans, especially in light of the slowing economy?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Then, I had asked the Government to flesh out the opportunities and pitfalls awaiting our local SMEs when the TPP is ratified.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I also suggested going at this in a big way, beyond communication with chambers of commerce and business federations, so as to encourage greater entrepreneurship amongst our people.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The TPP is likely to remain on the backburner at least until a new US President is sworn into office.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, the reality of not just TPP, but all future trade agreements should be considered with the launch of SkillsFuture and the national drive towards lifelong learning.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Trade agreements are sometimes conceived of as the domain of larger SMEs, multinational corporations (MNCs), tax agents and other specialists.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, it would be useful if the Government can identify areas of growth and greater access for enterprise under the TPP for Singapore, so that Singaporeans with the passion for enterprise and business can align their careers and skills upgrading plans to reap the benefits of our trade agreements.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I hope the Ministry can consider this and, at the very least, organise a webpage or similar public resource for such a purpose.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The services sector's share of the economy has been rising.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In recent quarters, with manufacturing in a recession and shedding jobs, it is the services sector that has held up the economy and prevented it from falling into a full-blown recession.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: One increasingly important aspect for the performance of the services sector is its exports.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This difference shows the potential which the services sector has in the future economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: How much of a concern are these developments for the Singapore economy?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Will we be able to exploit the opportunities offered by these agreements, specifically, not just to improve merchandise trade, but also services trade?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: So, my final question is: are the initiatives for promoting R&D and innovation coordinated with specific strategies to strengthen our trade performances in these areas?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With dynamism in the economy and growing regional competition, we need to take a multifaceted approach to develop an ecosystem that continuously creates jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As a start, I suggest we need a strategic outlook on what makes up this ecosystem and how to find traction within each of these spaces.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Logically, it begins with an end point of what potential industries we can attract or create in and out of Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As we move up the value chain and innovate within some of the traditional markets or industries, we can identify which we aspire to be in or in becoming a significant representation of.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As Mr Cedric Foo has pointed out, EDB has actively scouted for such partnerships in the past and created opportunities for the players to leverage our human capital in Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I think we need to accelerate this search for potential partners once again and create some cohorts of relevant talents in these fields.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With internationalisation, we should view our offices through a global lens.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The critical connection between Singaporeans and our work locations should be the people, and not the offices.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Our reputable Singapore brand gives us a notch in the international arena, and I think our younger generations should be adventurous in wanting to learn new skills and take opportunities beyond our local shores.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It is a different perspective, but one that strengthens our human capital and extends our job horizons over the years.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For more sustainable businesses, especially those in niche areas, it is necessary for us to generate end-to-end support functions in order to thrive.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Cost and labour are commonly some of the concerns and would foresee us not being a manufacturer in Singapore for some aspects.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But our role in the most critical levers within the ecosystem would be the value that we seek to position ourselves and transform ourselves into.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But manufacturing still has a very key role in our economy.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We should keep updating and strengthening our manufacturing sector to keep up with global trends: moving up the value chain and, especially, building and providing products to the world that other global cities are not able to or which would have difficulty matching us.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This seems a big aspiration, but it is also something that could bring us strategic value.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because high-end manufacturing supports an ecosystem of jobs and services, such as engineers and skilled workers, and many sectors that support innovation and technology that support the communities nearby.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We must also continue building a Singaporean Core with the necessary skills.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: SkillsFuture has great potential here as it helps get Singaporeans ready for the jobs of tomorrow.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But what about the industries of tomorrow, Mdm Chair?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In 2013, the McKinsey Global Institute published a report on disruptive technologies – an important global trend.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Technologies, such as: (a) additive manufacturing, 3D printing, which is going to disrupt supply chains around the world, because once it becomes easier to 3D print a part in the same town, you may not have to import it from further away; (b) cloud computing, which is going to disrupt the traditional market for local computer resources if you can use a cloud computer; (c) multi-touch interfaces that are disrupting the keyboard, mice and traditional input devices; and (d) automated knowledge work with intelligent assistants that can understand queries in natural language, whether it is the iPhone's Siri or the Cortana product that Microsoft has been working on.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: They may not have invented a Jarvis yet, but we can see these disrupting what is the work of a traditional personal assistant.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The McKinsey report mentions one key learning point which is very important to Singapore in my view: we maximise value creation when multiple disruptive technologies come together.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because when you put multi-touch screens, intelligent assistants, cloud computing together, you get something very similar to the iPhone or a Samsung smartphone.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, each technology could be an industry on its own, but it is together, when they converge, that they create transformative new markets.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: As we prepare for the future economy, we can position Singapore this way, bringing multiple innovations together; not just a hub, but a hub of hubs.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It can touch people from all walks of life.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: When recombinant DNA technology was invented many years ago, people thought it was an ivory tower invention.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Yet, today, it is fundamental to so many medical treatments, including the insulin injections that many diabetic patients rely on.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We should also incentivise companies to invest for the long term.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Clayton Christensen has written about "The Capitalist's Dilemma": short-term shareholders seeking short-term results.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, we should look at ways to encourage long-term investing, perhaps by aligning shareholder influence with shareholder duration.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: SMEs face developmental issues due to lack of resources and little access to information.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The use of big data in business is increasingly prevalent and will become de rigueur.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Big data can be used to predict footfall of customers at different times of the day, types of customers that frequent shops, time spent comparing products and even time spent at different parts of a store.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With such knowledge, retailers can play with product mix, price elasticity and store layout to maximise revenue.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With big data analysis, their ability to understand, predict and even direct customer behaviour will only increase.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we enable our SMEs to have access to the same information?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can we work with TACs and IHLs to do big data analysis on consumer behaviour and make available the analysis and public data banks so that our SMEs can leverage them to optimise their offerings and compete effectively?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This helps save cost for companies with respect to refrigeration, reduces spoilage during transformation, and increase marketability of products.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can we work with our TACs to keep our SMEs abreast of the packaging technology being researched on and provide them access to technology?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan
text: It is meant to push for change in the entire industry by working hand in hand with stakeholders at the organisational level.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan
text: It could turn out to be the type of penetrating approach which is needed to overcome resistance to transformation at the industry and firm level.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan
text: Similar, though not identical, industry-level schemes have worked elsewhere.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan
text: Nonetheless, I have some basic questions about whether overcoming a natural instinct of businesses to view businesses as competitors is possible and, even if it were possible, would it be worth the cost.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan
text: Improving the degree of industry-level coordination is key to the Industry Transformation Programme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan
text: Previous efforts, such as the Local Enterprise and Association Development (LEAD) programme, have shown what the potential challenges could be.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan
text: At the other end of the spectrum, there are also coordination challenges.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan
text: Is industry-level coordination capable of producing a level of cooperation that can be balanced against the natural competitive instinct?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan
text: As part of an open market economy, will the potential contradictions in seeking to coordinate entities which are supposed to be natural market-oriented competitors take an excessively heavy toll on the coordinating teams?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan
text: I understand that these coordinating teams will be formed from public servants from various agencies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan
text: So, will the coordination roles of these public servants result in public service agencies and personnel incurring heavy costs on resources?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan
text: And would it end up impacting the work of the Government?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Henry Kwek, you have two cuts, please take them together.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: My first cut is on the Industry Transformation Programme.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: As I have mentioned in my Budget speech, this is a bold and necessary move, one that will take Singapore into the next phase of economic development.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: During the recent debate on the President's Address, I shared my concerns that we must strengthen our startup ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Our outward-facing mainstream economy is facing intense global competition and we must quickly transit into the future economy as startups play an increasingly prominent role.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I look forward to hearing MTI's views on this matter.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Startups are like babies, so, I call them the babies of the industry.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I read an article which sums up the outcome of the Forbes Under 30 Summit in Tel Aviv held recently, which discussed the experiences and lessons learnt on startup companies, amongst many things.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It was noted that many startup companies fail, not because they had bad or good ideas, but mainly due to the process of execution.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The mistakes the companies made were that they are too focused on the big picture, the big idea and even the product itself and the broad concept.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: What they missed is spending time on turning the business plan into a thriving business.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: As the saying goes, "The devil always lies in the details".

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, we can see a growing number of startups recently, especially in the high-tech domain.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I believe it is a positive trend and I also believe they need a lot of support.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Apart from having a good idea and the will to venture and start his or her own company, these budding entrepreneurs should also be guided in execution of their business plan.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: In this light, start-ups can also learn from industry professionals who have the experience and knowledge in turning business plans into desired results.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Vice versa, we should also encourage industry professionals, companies and other voluntary organisations to come forward, participate and contribute to this new and growing trend.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The knowledge transfer from one to the other will not only benefit the startup, but also the nation at large.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even partial risk-sharing is still a risk to the bank.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And when there are other options for the banks to use their capital, such as lending to large corporates, risk-sharing may not be enough.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have heard from some SMEs that even if the bank has to bear less than 50% of the risk, many banks still behave as if that is a significant risk.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When applying for loans, many SMEs, even fairly large ones, still face high interest rates, small quantums, requests for personal security guarantees, or outright rejection on grounds, such as inconsistent revenues.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is there any survey evidence to suggest that SMEs feel that they are out of the woods in terms of access to finance?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The low-risk appetite of banks and lack of credit information on SMEs could be one cause.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In Germany and Japan, countries with vibrant SMEs, links between regional banks and regional companies are critical to ensure access to capital.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Other countries also have Export-Import (EXIM) banks suggested by the Economics Strategies Committee in 2010.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: An EXIM bank with a clear mandate could have provided finance to SMEs to tap on the regional market of over three billion people to grow and become competitive.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Workers' Party has, in the past, called for the EXIM bank idea to be reexamined with a focus on SMEs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is vital that we maximise our returns from our R&D spend, a critical investment that takes a significant share of our budget expenditure even as our fiscal position gets tighter.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I support the Government's sharpened focus on growing our capabilities in research translation, innovation and facilitating startups, so that research and innovation can be applied to our economic and social needs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Germany has a robust system of applying R&D to drive innovations in their businesses.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: One factor that facilitates this is the practice where professors at German universities often hold concurrent appointments overseeing R&D at industry groups, allowing for seamless testing and implementation of research initiatives.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: How will the Government support linkages across R&D value chains to bring technology inventions from the laboratories into our industries and grow strong industry clusters?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I would also like to ask the Minister for his insights on the performance of R&D in the various sectors and how such insights will help guide future Government funding support, including how SMEs can tap on the RIE2020 to drive innovation and scale up their businesses.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: At the very least, we should own IP rights which are of strategic value to Singapore.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: My point was simple: without ownership, we do not have the liberty to own, use and exploit such IP for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: If ownership flows out of Singapore, we not only lose the opportunity for value creation, growth and revenue, we run the risk of being rendered obsolete.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We must, therefore, have safeguards against the inadvertent use of our funds and resources to equip our competitors.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: There is much that we can learn and benefit from such collaborations.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: All I am saying is that in giving and taking, we must know what we want to take for what we are willing to give.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, I would also prefer very much that grantees of Government funds for purposes of research and innovation would use the IP that they own and grant licences to the Government for national applications.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Economic impact and community impact – we have a lot of talk about that.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We need to know what the measurable outcomes should be – long-term, mid-term, short-term, tangible, intangible.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, I would like to know the guidelines and principles, applied and to be applied in the settings of key performance indicators (KPIs).

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I would also request to know what the consequences of not meeting KPIs may be.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I wish to highlight the importance that R&D can play for SMEs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the case of Japan, with its shrinking workforce, we have witnessed how crucial R&D has been for not only sustaining the workforce with innovations to boost productivity, but also inventing new technologies that are admired and sold worldwide.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As a small country, we have limited manpower and natural resources.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Other countries with more resources are always going to do better when it comes to mainstream products and services.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our SMEs must rise above the crowd with unique selling points and innovative products and services, and that can only be achieved through R&D.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But R&D may be costly and may not be easily accessible for some.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Social robotics is now a recognised field that has spawned industry conferences, global collaboration and much investment.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I am aware that social robotics is far from new to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Late last year, the Nanyang Technological University (NTU) unveiled Nadine, a life-size robot.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: A*Star Social Robotics Laboratory was launched in 2008.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: In the eldercare space, I must stress that social robots should never replace genuine and loving human contact from family, friends and caregivers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Having said that, social robots could be designed to interact with older Singaporeans in various languages.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: They can also monitor vital signs, help dispense medicine, answer questions verbally, help connect phone calls, obtain emergency help and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: In the preschool space, social robots could complement the vital role of teachers in the classroom and provide an amusing and engaging way for children to learn and also receive classroom assistance.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: This might help raise the productivity and effectiveness of our preschool teachers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: An example is KASPAR, a social robot designed by the University of Hertfordshire in the United Kingdom (UK) to help children with autism learn responses from the robot through games and interactive play.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Low Thia Khiang, you have three cuts.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Both Indonesia and Vietnam have mooted plans to build nuclear power plants.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: If Indonesia builds a nuclear power plant, there is always a possibility that an earthquake could cause a disaster on the scale of Fukushima and the weather patterns and ocean currents would bring the nuclear fallout to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Even without natural disasters, a nuclear plant located anywhere in the region would produce a large amount of nuclear waste that would need to be disposed of.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: This waste is significantly radioactive and would take tens of thousands of years to be rendered safe.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Extremely stringent security must be in place to ensure that this waste does not fall into the hands of terrorists.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The waste can be used to make a so-called "dirty" bomb, which would be a very effective weapon of terror.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: This is not a remote threat, as Prime Minister Lee has revealed at the Nuclear Security Summit in Washington that Singapore authorities have intercepted a cargo with nuclear material.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: It is good to know that the Government has tightened its export control regime, upgraded radiation-screening technology at the ports and is building a border laboratory.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The National Research Foundation created a five-year programme in 2014 to conduct research and education into nuclear safety, science and engineering.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Could the Government give an update on the progress of the programme and the results?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: While gas-fired plants are among the most efficient and gas is the cleanest fossil fuel, with more countries importing liquefied natural gas (LNG), we are going to face more competition for LNG sources.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: This heavy dependency on natural gas opens us to risks of spikes in prices and disruption of supplies.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: In the medium to long term, what is the status of other energy options that we are looking at to further diversify our energy mix to improve our energy security?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The ASEAN Power Grid (APG) has been mooted in 1997 under the ASEAN Vision 2020 towards ensuring regional energy security while promoting the efficient utilisation and sharing of resources.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Would we be able to tap on these energy resources under the programme?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: What is the current status of the APG project?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Currently, electricity tariffs are calculated based on fuel oil prices.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: In the past, when the rationale for linking our electricity tariffs to fuel oil prices was that there was no distinct market in Asia for the price of natural gas, hence, indexing its price to fuel oil prices is the next best alternative.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Earlier this year, the Singapore Exchange (SGX) started up a new index for LNG known as SLInG, which provides an industry pricing benchmark.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Should we consider now factoring in the LNG Price Index in our formula for electricity tariffs to better reflect the actual costs of power generation?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: (In Mandarin):   Singapore has progressively opened the retail electricity market since 2001.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: As at today, there are 890,000 users who can choose their own electricity suppliers, ranging from large-scale plants to small shops.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The Energy Market Authority (EMA) launched the Electricity Vending System as early as 2007.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: In 2010, EMA launched a trial of the Intelligent Energy System, and in 2012, it rolled out Phase 2 of the trial in Punggol New Town.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: During the COS debate in 2013, Ms Sylvia Lim had enquired about the above trial.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: She had asked if there are plans to fully liberalise the retail electricity market in the near term.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: At that time, the Minister only elaborated on the sophisticated technology involved, but did not reveal the results of the trial and the operation of the system.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: They will be able to choose the electricity price package, just like choosing a mobile phone service package.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The full liberalisation of the market in 2018 may be good for the domestic users.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: However, if they do not understand how the retail electricity market operates, they may not be able to choose a price package that will help them save on their electricity bills.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: As this change will impact our entire population, does the Government have any plans to kick-start the publicity campaign earlier, so that people have enough time to digest the news?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The difference between domestic users and commercial users is that one may need to communicate with domestic users in a language other than English.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Are authorities well-prepared to roll out the publicity in different languages?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, it is important that we plan ahead and find more sustainable ways to cater to our energy consumption.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked about the global economic outlook and the implications for Singapore's economy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: The global economic recovery has been weaker than expected and the IMF has again downgraded its global growth forecasts.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: It has done so almost every year since the Global Financial Crisis.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: We are now in a paradigm of slower growth, compared to the previous decade.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Meanwhile, there are significant global rebalancing forces that must work themselves through over the next three to five years.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: First, the key developed economies have been implementing loose monetary policy through measures, such as quantitative easing and low interest rates, in an attempt to revive their economies.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Some of them have even introduced negative interest rates.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: This is unsustainable in the long run and these economies will have to normalise their monetary policies at some point.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: As the monetary policies normalise, it will affect financial and currency markets as well as capital flows around the world, especially in emerging economies.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Second, the reforms in China are creating a "new normal".

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Besides rebalancing towards consumption and services-led growth, China has also been increasingly in-sourcing the intermediate goods and services required to produce its manufacturing output, rather than importing them.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: While China is making this transition, the countries which trade with China will also be affected because supply chains will have to adjust.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: In Singapore, we will need to find new growth niches in order to remain relevant as China makes its adjustments.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Third, in commodity markets, there has been an oversupply of oil in the global market due to over-investment, leading to a sharp drop in oil prices.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: With growth in global oil demand expected to remain weak, further adjustments in global oil supply will have to be made.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: As a result, there may be continued uncertainties surrounding oil prices.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: In addition, we will face structural adjustments domestically because of our demographics and ageing population.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: The local workforce will continue to grow, but at a slower rate than before as more Baby Boomers approach retirement age.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Overall workforce growth will be around 1%-2% per annum for the rest of the decade.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: While all sectors will have to adjust to the tighter supply of labour, labour-intensive services sectors, such as food services, will likely be more adversely affected.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: The factors above point to an uncertain economic environment for the next few years.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: When we are on a slow growth trajectory of 1%-3%, some sectors will grow more strongly than the 1%-3% range and some sectors will be below the 1%-3% range.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: As Mr Liang Eng Hwa observed, this means that, for some sectors, they are contracting and feel like they are in a recession.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: This is one of the consequences of a low-growth trajectory.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: And that is why we are also addressing the challenges at the sectoral level.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Given the current global economic outlook, Mr Liang asked how the Government will help companies ride through this difficult period.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: The Government is watching the situation very closely and we are prepared to take further action, if necessary.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: We remain committed to working with companies to overcome these challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Mr Leon Perera asked whether the loan scheme would sufficiently incentivise the banks to extend loans when they otherwise would not.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: The second broad thrust is to provide more support to help companies restructure and transform as well as develop critical capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: One way is through the Automation Support Package, which can help companies to improve their productivity by scaling up through automation adoption.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: The third broad thrust is through the provision of infrastructure.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: The needs of the different sectors are quite diverse.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: JTC has, therefore, developed a pipeline of innovative developments for the various sectors to better cater to their different needs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Others, like the Food Hub @ Senoko, Furniture Hub @ Sungei Kadut and Logistics Hub @ Gul, will be ready in the next few years, and were developed together with the trade associations and companies to ensure that they meet the specific needs of these sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Companies should, therefore, take this opportunity to consider regrouping and consolidating their space and land requirements, and leverage these new facilities to achieve better operational efficiency and higher productivity.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Such transformation will require deep partnerships between the Government and industry, and among the industry players to develop a more competitive sectoral response.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: First, strengthen leadership within TACs, such as through consultancy support for strategic plan development.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Second, build capability in TAC secretariats, including training to manage corporate functions.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Third, develop robust processes, particularly in the areas of human resource, information technology and finance, and enhance their branding of TACs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Fourth, enhance TACs' ability to provide services to companies, such as market research and technology mapping.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: For example, the Waste Management and Recycling Association Singapore (WMRAS) led a project to encourage the mass adoption of automated canvas covers for the trucks used in waste collection.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: A total of six service providers were engaged to pilot this adoption for 39 companies in the waste management industry.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Minister of State Koh Poh Koon will elaborate on our partnership with TACs when he responds on the segment on SMEs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Mr Cedric Foo asked about our foreign investment attraction strategy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: We have adopted a targeted approach towards attracting foreign investments that take into account our competitive advantage, growth opportunities as well as constraints in manpower, land and planned international commitments on carbon emissions.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: For example, we will continue to pursue opportunities arising from growth drivers, including the rise of consumerism and urbanisation in Asia.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Our investments in advanced manufacturing capabilities, such as robotics, 3D printing and digital manufacturing, will also position our manufacturing sector well for the future.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: More importantly, our efforts must translate into good job opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: We have a comprehensive suite of manpower development initiatives, in partnership with the industry and the Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs), to ensure that our workforce has the right skillsets to take up the new jobs that have been created.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Parliamentary Secretary Low Yen Ling will elaborate on this later.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Beyond attracting companies to Singapore, we are also working to establish stronger trade linkages to support Singapore companies looking to expand overseas.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan asked about our 2015 services trade performance and the opportunities from the AEC as well as TPP.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: While our services trade balance is, indeed, negative, the deficit has generally narrowed over the past 10 years.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: The slowdown in Singapore's services export growth in 2015 was in line with the weakening global trade environment.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Nevertheless, amidst this slowdown, we observed that export growth in the financial services as well as telecommunications, computer and information services sectors remained healthy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Over the longer term, the outlook for these services sectors remains promising, given the rise of the middle class and urbanisation in regional economies like ASEAN.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Specifically, AEC and TPP will provide opportunities for us to expand the reach of Singapore's services exports and facilitate services trade flows to our major services export markets.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Mr Cedric Foo and Mr Pritam Singh asked about the benefits of AEC and TPP to Singaporeans and Singapore companies.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: AEC will benefit Singapore companies over a broad spectrum of sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Virtually all goods now flow throughout the ASEAN region tariff-free.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: This allows our businesses to trade and gain market access into the region while bearing practically zero customs duties.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Restrictions have also been eased in at least 80 services sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: ASEAN countries now allow majority foreign ownership in many sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Along with ASEAN's commitments to facilitate, promote, protect and liberalise cross-border investments, Singapore companies can now venture into the region at lower costs and with greater investment protection.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: The engineering services sector provides a useful example of how our companies can benefit from AEC.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Singapore companies can now own a 100% stake in Indonesia's engineering design and advisory services, as well as in Myanmar's engineering and construction services sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Our companies can also benefit from legally-binding guarantees of preferential services market access in the ASEAN region.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: The tighter the regional integration, the stronger our value proposition as a gateway to ASEAN.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Therefore, as a small country, Singapore must adopt an inclusionary approach towards trade agreements.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: This is why we are a founding member of key trade agreements like the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP), TPP and the eventual Free Trade Area of the Asia Pacific (FTAAP).

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Being part of such agreements allows us to influence the rules of engagement and, where possible, enables us to enhance demand of manufactured goods and services from Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: For example, despite the fact that we have the US-Singapore FTA (USSFTA), few of our automotive parts manufacturers would export to the US today.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: In other sectors, such as textiles, our companies, likewise, have difficulties utilising the US-Singapore FTA to enter the US market at a preferential rate, because too little of the raw materials are being produced in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Our garment manufacturers can, therefore, look forward to sourcing more competitively from the TPP region and focus on keeping the high-value aspects of production in Singapore, knowing that their exports will now enjoy a comparative advantage because of this "regional cumulation" effect.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: This is a very significant development, especially for our SMEs in the textile and garment sector.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: We will work closely with our TACs and our economic agencies will develop more sector-specific outreach sessions.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: The SkillsFuture movement will prepare Singaporeans to take advantage of the evolving job landscape and opportunities provided by these regional economic integration efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Specific sector plans will be targeted at upskilling workers in both the traditional areas, such as retail, as well as the emerging areas, such as finance technology, or Fintech.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: MTI is one of the key agencies supporting SkillsFuture and we will continue to work with the various Government agencies to support our companies and workers.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: This includes our strong legal and physical infrastructure, our well-diversified economy and an educated workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: We need to build on these strengths and continue to implement measures to stay competitive.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: That is why it is timely to reiterate the key principles that will continue to remain relevant in the years to come.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: First of all, as a small economy, we must remain open and connected to grow the external wing of our economy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Our external economy can continue to contribute significantly to our GDP and good jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: So, we must look at opportunities that lie beyond our shores in markets, such as ASEAN and beyond.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Second, we need to leverage the small size of our economy to our advantage and be more nimble, adaptable and flexible.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: We must adapt to changes brought about by the rebalancing of the global economy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: We cannot simply remain business-as-usual and we cannot be afraid of change, or we will be left behind.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: As the global economy rebalances, we will continue to work with businesses to stay the course on economic transformation and ensure that Singapore remains attractive to foreign investments.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Our economic growth strategies will enable us to seize regional as well as global opportunities to create more value.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Together, we can continue to create good jobs for Singaporeans and ensure that we are well-positioned for the future.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: They have raised a wide range of questions which I will now endeavour to address.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Miss Cheryl Chan has asked about our strategy to generate sustainable economic growth and create good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This, in fact, is the focus of CFE, which Mr Liang Eng Hwa enquired about.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We have done so previously with the Economic Review Committee in 2001; and the Economic Strategies Committee in 2009.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: And this resolute focus on the long term has really been our hallmark, you could say even our competitive advantage, in the way we have worked on the economy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In consultation with industry leaders, the CFE is studying the trends that will underpin the next wave of growth markets and sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: And it is a national effort to understand the threats and opportunities these trends present, and what we need, in this next phase, in terms of corporate capabilities, connectivity, infrastructure and skills so that we can sustain our economy well into the future.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: They are disrupting industry structures and value chains and also changing the nature of jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: China's in-sourcing of intermediate goods and services, similar trends in the US in terms of re-shoring, will have a major impact on distributed manufacturing networks and cross-border supply chains.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Meanwhile, India, ASEAN and other emerging markets have a growing middle class that is demanding more and sophisticated products and services.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: New technologies are blurring traditional industry boundaries and creating hybrid sectors like Fintech.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: For example, if you look at 3D printing and advanced robotics, they can revolutionise manufacturing.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The impact is in terms of rapid prototyping, optimised design and vastly improved efficiencies.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Digital technologies, such as big data, Internet-of-Things (IoT), artificial intelligence, and Cloud, these enable innovation and new business models to access markets and address evolving preferences of consumers anywhere in the world at any time.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In fact, there is an article on this today in The Straits Times, with big data and predictive analytics allowing retailers to better target customers in whichever market.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: These changes, coupled with our domestic constraints, affect different sectors differently.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: An enterprise level response, while necessary, is not sufficient, given the nature and the scale of these challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: So, we need broader sector-focused strategies that systematically harness innovation, talent development and partnerships, to sustain the competitiveness and growth of our economy and industries.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: And that is the essential thrust of the Industry Transformation Programme.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: I want to illustrate using the manufacturing sector.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng commented on its strategic value and Mr Yee Chia Hsing asked for the Government's view on its importance.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: That is a compound annual growth rate of about 1.4%.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: But that was due to the impact on one or two particular sectors, especially offshore and marine, due to the oil-related impact.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Manufacturing productivity is also higher and has grown faster than the overall economy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: And manufacturing, which employs more than half a million people, continues to provide good jobs not just in the sector alone, but in related areas like R&D, after-sales services and distribution.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In 2015, more than 60% – six out of 10 – of the resident workers in the sector were in skilled jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This is higher again than the overall economy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Median wages in the manufacturing sector are also higher than that for the overall economy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In addition, the sector generates healthy spillover benefits for the rest of the economy, through its wide range of industry inter-linkages.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: For all these reasons, manufacturing remains important to our economy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: But the nature of manufacturing is changing and we must undertake several measures to ensure that the sector is well-positioned for the future.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: First, we want to invest in advanced manufacturing technologies, such as additive manufacturing and robotics, and also promote their adoption across different verticals.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The global robotics industry is projected to grow from about US$27 billion last year to about US$80 billion in 2025.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This will include public-private partnerships among research institutions, companies and public agencies, to pilot robotics technology applications across various industries.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We will support the mass adoption of robotics across sectors to drive productivity.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: These are important upfront work that we need to do in order to not just come up with solutions, but encourage its adoption.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Mr Leon Perera would be interested to note that there are potential robotics applications in the services sector that are currently being worked on in Singapore to automate manual tasks, raise productivity and address manpower challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In eldercare, the use of assistive technology can ease the burden on healthcare professionals and caregivers, and nursing homes, such as Peacehaven, are already exploring possible applications.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: So, if you go there, you may not see it because it is operating at the back-of-house.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: But there are plans to take it further to the front-of-house for the delivery of luggage or room service to guests.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The adoption of robotics in areas where you have human interface, what Mr Leon Perera called social robots, would take more effort.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Precisely because of the human interface, a lot more effort needs to be done, in terms of how you calibrate these devices in order to serve their purpose and to be able to respond.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: But there are significant efforts being made and part of it is, of course, what we are trying to do in some of these verticals.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: It is expanding the notion of manufacturing and we are working with the industry to capture those opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Medical technology firms are using analytics – Members have talked about it – to go beyond producing medical devices to providing digital healthcare solutions.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: So, they are enlarging the value proposition, such as the remote monitoring of medical conditions.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: EDB also worked with Philips to establish its Asia-Pacific Centre of Excellence for its hospital-to-home business units in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This is an example of how a firm that was in manufacturing of medical technology (medtech) is also moving into larger solutions or related service activities which complement manufacturing.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This is something we want to work on and there are other examples in aviation, aeronautics and so on.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng highlighted the need to bring together the industries and disruptive technologies of tomorrow.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: I think this is very important because many new opportunities actually lie precisely at this confluence of different industries and new technologies.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This rich ecosystem has spawned many collaborative projects in biomedical sciences, infocommunications, physical sciences and engineering.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: It will host the entire value chain, which will include R&D, design, prototyping, production and supply chain management, and have access to NTU's research and engineering capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: But ultimately, Chairman, we must ensure that our people benefit from these changes and the opportunities, as Dr Tan Wu Meng has emphasised.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Under SkillsFuture, the tripartite partners are working closely with education and training institutions to equip Singaporeans with the requisite skillsets under various sectoral manpower plans.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: One example of a Singaporean who has acquired new skills to meet the needs of his industry is Mohd Jamil Bin Mohd Said from Sanwa-Sayama Precision Engineering Pte Ltd.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Jamil joined Sanwa in 1998 as a technician specialising in mold-making.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is a very good example and there are many others like him.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We need similar efforts across all sectors and Parliamentary Secretary Low Yen Ling will elaborate further.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Members would have noted that partnerships are central to these industry transformation efforts.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan asked whether such coordination and cooperation can be balanced with the natural competitive instincts of an open-market economy.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: On the face of it, Chairman, this inherent tension seems irreconcilable.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Last year, PACT was enhanced to support activities like joint product development between larger enterprises and their suppliers.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We have also brought together competitors in collaborative projects.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: An example of that is A*STAR's Aerospace Research Consortium, which brings together Airbus, Boeing and Embraer, to undertake pre-competitive research into complex problems facing the industry.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is not just about collaboration with the Government, but also within the private sector.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: More companies are embracing the idea of open innovation and working collaboratively.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: They are born out of the recognition that even competitors stand to benefit when they cooperate in certain parts of the business process, either because it is an area which is very complex or where the barrier costs are very high.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, a collective effort tends to achieve a much better outcome and they can all share in it.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Henry Kwek and Assoc Prof Randolph Tan asked how the Industry Transformation Programme differs from our current approach.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: At the enterprise level, the Government will continue to support our companies in their innovation, productivity, skills upgrading and internationalisation efforts.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: However, as I have mentioned and we have heard in the comments by many Members, the nature of the current trends and challenges is such that it calls for broader strategies at the sectoral level.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We need measures which the market may not be ready to supply or adopt.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Take, for example, the case of modularised robotics solutions.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We could call this market failure or perhaps market gap.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We will need to act proactively in order to generate the solutions which can be adopted.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Under the Industry Transformation Programme, what we can do is bring stakeholders and our resources together, with scale and focus to proactively support each sector's development and response to the differing challenges that they face.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And we do not underestimate the scale of this challenge.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is a point that several Members have made.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Industry Transformation is challenging and will require deep partnerships among large and small companies, public research institutions and private enterprises as well as TACs and, of course, Government agencies.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Centres of innovation, for example, will have a view on the technology landscape.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: TACs will have a better grasp of industry trends and what the needs of their members are.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Unions will have a view on how skills training and workforce development can take place.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We need to bring all these together to address some of the most salient issues in the medium to long term for our sectors.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: To coordinate and execute the industry transformation effort, we will appoint "cluster champions" from agencies like EDB, SPRING and IE Singapore.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But they are not the only ones, because there are other agencies looking at different sectors.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I understand Assoc Prof Randolph Tan's fears that this might impose an excessive administrative burden.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: However, based on our experience, the plans that are being formulated should result in a tighter coordination of efforts and a more effective use of our resources.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We will have to implement and work on this, and it is going to be an iterative process as we go forward.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Tan is the owner of a local medium-size food manufacturer, with plans to automate and increase production for export.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: He engages a system integrator to study the automation project, with a consultancy and installation fee of $200,000.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: He then invests $1.8 million to purchase three robotic arms and a conveyor belt system that integrates the packing and palletising process.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And as Members know, the Government's risk-share has been increased from 50% to 70% for SMEs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This should improve Mr Tan's chances of securing a competitive loan.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: With the capacity to scale production, he can also tap on IE Singapore's schemes, such as the Market Readiness Assistance and Global Company Partnerships, in order to go overseas.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, taken together, this is a package which will deliver substantial benefits to SMEs that are prepared to take the decision to automate.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That decision will also give SMEs the capacity to think about going overseas and entering new markets, for which there are also support schemes available.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Entrepreneurship and innovation are two important enablers of this.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Henry Kwek asked about the progress of our efforts to develop a startup ecosystem.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Our startups have also attracted more investor interest, which is one measure of their quality.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The number as well as the value of these venture capital funded transactions have been significant in the startup space.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Importantly, our efforts to nurture the startup ecosystem have allowed budding entrepreneurs to fulfil their aspirations.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: She is the co-founder and CEO of Peregrine Ophthalmic, a local biotech start-up.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: With SPRING's support and, together with co-founders, Deputy President and provost of NTU, Prof Freddy Boey, and Chair of the School of Material Science and Engineering at NTU, Prof Subbu Venkatraman, Assoc Prof Wong has developed the world's first sustained-release nanomedicine for ophthalmology for the treatment of glaucoma.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Henry Kwek also asked about the Government's future plans to support the growth of startups in Singapore.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We plan to support the startup ecosystem by supporting innovative companies to scale through: (a) internationalisation; (b) partnerships; (c) an enabling regulatory environment; and (d) talent development.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: There are more and more opportunities for a startup to scale through digital internationalisation.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Indeed, you could say that many of these companies are born global because, from the moment they start, they can access international markets.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: BeMyGuest (BMG) is a local startup that recently became the first Singaporean company to be featured on Fast Company's "World's 50 Most Innovative Companies List 2016" for its online travel platform.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: IE Singapore supported this company in its digital integration with Ctrip, China's largest online travel agency.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This has allowed BMG to establish tie-ups with 25 other Chinese partners and increase bookings by over 100 times in a period of nine months.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That is the power of digital access to markets.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And this year, the company is also working with IE Singapore to penetrate other Asian markets, such as Japan, India, Indonesia and Korea.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: SPRING and IE Singapore will continue to support our companies, especially the startups, to build capabilities in these areas, such as customer analytics, social media marketing, mobile commerce and digital platform development, to benefit from the global digital economy.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: What we see more and more of are large enterprises embracing open innovation to access new technologies and ideas.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
