text: EDB and SPRING have, in fact, been working with many MNCs and large local enterprises (LLEs) to undertake corporate incubation and venture activities, as well as co-innovation partnerships with our startups.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: What this means is that with such partnerships, our startups will have the financial resources, expertise and networks to scale.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: On regulatory environment, let me use the medtech industry as an example.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The Health Sciences Authority (HSA) has been adopting a risk-based approach to the regulation of medical devices by ensuring that the controls commensurate with the risk of the devices to individual health.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: HSA has also expedited approvals for devices that have been cleared by reference agencies.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: More recently, they have introduced an online Medical Device Risk Classification Tool, which allows companies to quickly identify the risk classification of a medical device within five to 10 minutes.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is important because the risk classification tells them the kind of regulatory hurdles they face.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And these five to 10 minutes, to put it in context, are much faster than the previous one to two weeks of paper-based processing.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: HSA and many of our other regulators are exploring how we can create an enabling environment without compromising their core regulatory objectives.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Azmoon Ahmad asked about our efforts to nurture entrepreneurs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We will continue to provide support for mentorship through initiatives, such as SPRING's Incubator Development Programme (IDP).

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Under IDP, incubators and accelerators are supported with grants to enhance their capabilities and programmes, including the engagement of mentors.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is something we can scale according to the needs and responses.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I agree fully with Ms Foo Mee Har and Ms Chia Yong Yong who emphasised the need to ensure that value is created for Singapore from our $19 billion investment in RIE2020, and our broader investments in R&D.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Our investments in R&D have strengthened our innovation ecosystem and created value for Singapore.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That is a significant increase and, importantly, 70% of those jobs are held by locals.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, we have been able to grow our local capacity as well.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, on the one hand, the businesses have been catalysed to spend more on R&D, and we also see a commensurate enhancement in our capacity, especially in the local talent pool, to meet those needs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Importantly, our R&D investments have also enabled new industries to grow.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: As a reference, if I remember correctly, in 2000, VA from the BMS sector was about $4 billion.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: To assure Members, we also have a framework to track the KPI of our R&D investments.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: These range from input measures, such as R&D intensity and researcher intensity, relative to comparable economies so that we have some benchmarking, to measures of the quality of the research, such as citations and papers published, and measures of value creation, which several Members have talked about, through commercialisation, including licensing and spinoffs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Ms Chia asked about the treatment of IP ownership arising from R&D activities.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In general, A*STAR retains ownership of the IPs that it develops; where an IP is jointly developed with a collaborator, including from the private sector, the IP may be jointly-owned.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And we have multiple mechanisms to facilitate the use and commercialisation of that IP later on.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Licensing is one, but there are other mechanisms.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Beyond the licensing of IPs, we also have longer-term initiatives to align our R&D investments with the needs of companies and the economy.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The Industry Alignment Fund (IAF), which was introduced under RIE2015, seeks to tighten the linkages between R&D capabilities and the industry's needs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We are trying to bring the research in our institutes closer to industry, and IAF is one mechanism to do that.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: IAF has supported about 600 projects to date.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: These projects were carried out in collaboration with industry by our public sector research institutes and also pertain to developing capabilities needed by the industry.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We are adding to that Fund because that is where we want to emphasise the R&D efforts in the way it is aligned with the industry.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The IAF is also being adapted to meet the changing needs of industry, which are becoming more complex and need to tap on a diverse spectrum of capabilities.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: For example, Nestle sees opportunities in combining traditional food manufacturing with sophisticated biomedical knowledge, especially on nutrition and formulations.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The Nestle Research Centre Asia was established here to leverage A*STAR's research capabilities to develop new nutritional products.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We will allocate about $660 million to this form of IAF-Industry Collaboration Projects, which will draw on the best researchers and capabilities across our public sector research community.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And this goes to the point about what we expect in return – we require tangible contributions from industry partners in cash, in terms of the resources they commit and the longevity of that commitment, as a measure of their commitment to the projects and the projects' relevance to industry.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Very often, these commitments are also in parallel with other kinds of activities the industry partners are undertaking in Singapore.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I just want to make one final point on this.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I know this was not the intent of Ms Chia Yong Yong's comment.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The Member qualified it but I would like to restate it.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We should be cautious not to adopt a parochial attitude towards innovation or the ownership of IP.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That is a very important thing to bear in mind.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Some of the best outcomes in innovation are produced when it is undertaken in an open and collaborative manner.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We must preserve that environment in our R&D ecosystem.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Hence, we must maintain an open innovation ecosystem that fosters collaboration among multiple stakeholders, whether they are public or private, large or small, local or foreign.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Such R&D activities bring many other valuable benefits to Singapore which I have enumerated.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Ms Foo Mee Har, Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Ms Sun Xueling rightly pointed out that innovation should play a key role in the push for our SMEs to transform.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And we will enhance SMEs' access to technologies and expertise.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So far, they have matched, I am told, more than 70 companies.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Through SPRING's network amongst SMEs and TACs, I think the level of technology transfer that is relevant to the needs of SMEs is going to be significantly improved.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: There is also an initiative to simplify licensing terms for SMEs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I was very pleased to learn that A*STAR's licensing agreements are now shorter and use simpler language.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We can all do with simpler language and it has reduced the time required for licensing significantly.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We will also do more – and I think this is something that is noteworthy for Members – to grow the in-house innovation capabilities of our SMEs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: A*STAR and SPRING's GET-Up Programme actually seconds our public researchers in our IHLs, research institutes and polytechnics to SMEs to undertake innovation projects.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, they become the employees of that company to work on their research blueprint, in order to develop particular solutions.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In many cases, they have gone on to become commercially valuable.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Under RIE2020, we will enhance the programme to second senior research scientists and engineers (RSEs) to SMEs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Low Thia Khiang asked about the Government's plans to enhance and diversify our energy sources.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We have taken significant steps in this regard.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Our LNG terminal, which commenced operations in 2013, allows us to geographically diversify our sources of natural gas, which is our main source of energy.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Just to take up Mr Low's point, you could say that we are intensifying our use of LNG.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But what we are actually doing with the LNG terminal is diversifying geographically our sources of natural gas.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: There are some questions on renewables which Parliamentary Secretary Ms Low Yen Ling will take up.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We are also studying the feasibility of electricity imports in the medium to long term.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That is where the ASEAN Power Grid is relevant.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is really a plan to have a network of the grid infrastructure for an integrated ASEAN electricity market.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: To date, Members may not be surprised to hear that six of the 16 planned bilateral interconnection projects have been completed, including one between Singapore and Peninsular Malaysia.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Low Thia Khiang asked about the potential impact to Singapore should our neighbours embark on a nuclear power programme.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The pre-feasibility study, which the Member noted was completed in 2012, concluded that the currently available nuclear energy technologies were not yet suitable for deployment in Singapore.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: However, we are strengthening our capabilities to understand nuclear science and technology to allow us to assess the implications for Singapore of evolving nuclear energy technologies and regional nuclear energy developments.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It comprises the Singapore Nuclear Research and Safety Initiative focusing on research and developing capabilities in nuclear safety science and engineering, and the Nuclear Education and Training Fund to support education and training in these areas.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It works on a wide range of areas and I am happy to furnish more information.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But so far, four of the research projects have commenced in 2015 and the remaining five are expected to commence in 2016.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In terms of scholarships, so far, nine scholarships have been awarded.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Low Thia Khiang commented that it is lower than expected.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Well, the only comment that I would make is that this is a rather specialised field.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is not so easy to get people in their applications to say, "Let's take up the scholarship to go and do nuclear studies".

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: What we have done is to reach out to try and attract students to take this up, and we will continue to invest in these efforts significantly.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Importantly, it is also about working together with other nuclear technology partners in other established venues like in France and the US and so on, which adds to our knowledge and ability to build up the core of Singapore-based capabilities to understand this space.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is both on aspects of operations as well as issues of disposal of nuclear waste which Mr Low Thia Khiang mentioned.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Low Thia Khiang has asked if electricity prices can be delinked from oil and linked to natural gas or LNG instead.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is quite ironic because, right now, we actually have lower electricity prices because of lower oil prices.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, we should be careful what we wish for.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Having said that, the crux of the matter is not about picking which is going to be cheaper because, at some point, oil prices may be low; at other times, it may be high, and we will see a similar impact on gas prices.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: What we really want to do is to allow options in Singapore where the buyers of gas have the opportunity to create a portfolio which they think best suits their risk appetite and hedges against the movements that they are concerned about.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, SLInG, which Mr Low highlighted, is one possibility.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is very new and not quite ready yet for that sort of indexing, but we think that it has potential and we have to see how the market responds.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: There is also the question of full retail contestability.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Having said that, I want to make two points.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, that is what the work is on now.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The system is not just about the technical aspects but also the potential suppliers, how they will come in and what kind of packages they offer.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: These are some of the policy aspects that are being worked out.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Once we are ready, we will embark on an education programme to socialise our households to the opportunities.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The key is that we have all parties on board in order to achieve the objectives that we have set for ourselves.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Chairman, and fellow Members, trade associations (TAs) can play an important role in helping SMEs and traditional industries to be future-ready.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Many TA leaders are dedicating their services to their TAs while managing their businesses.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Although companies compete amongst themselves in businesses, everyone in their TA stands united and works hand in hand for the common interests and with the goal of enhancing the overall image of the industry.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The motivation behind it is passion and a "never-say-die" mindset.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: However, we have to acknowledge that no one can stop its evolution.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Traditional industries need to move with the times and make adjustments proactively.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The first is the Singapore Precision Engineering and Technology Association (SPETA), renamed from "Tooling" to "Technology".

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The second is the Singapore Houseware Association, which was renamed from "Chinaware" to "Houseware".

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The change of name provides broader scope for these TAs.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Another example is the Singapore Industrial Automation Association.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: They did not change their name, but repositioned themselves through their events.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Their conference and exhibition were named ioTAsia, with "ioT" being the "Internet of things", a very modern technology terminology.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: To effectively promote the collaboration between the Government and TAs, I would like to highlight two dilemmas of TA leaders.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: TAs are non-profit organisations and have limited operational funds.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: With the support of the Government, some projects which have shown initial good results would see Government officers being over-eager to deliver the KPIs, to the extent of even bypassing the TAs and taking over the projects via setting up new entities.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: However, those TAs with limited resources but which work hard in search of new directions can only fend for themselves although they need even more assistance.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: This situation takes place probably because Government officers have a preconceived notion, that is, supporting TAs that they deem promising and not wanting to waste time on TAs that they feel would not be able to make it.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: I need to reiterate that bringing up these two dilemmas does not affect TAs' support and expectations of Government policies.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: As the President of the Singapore Chinese Chamber of Commerce and Industry (SCCCI), I am heartened that the Chamber's TA Hub has received the strong support of many Government agencies and TA members.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: We hope to provide the various TAs with a platform and space to better lead their respective industries.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, we hope that the TA leaders from the different industries can meet one another more often, creating chemistry for new business and new opportunities.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, after listening to the speeches in Parliament over the past few days, I fully agree with the union leaders who called for companies and employees to move with the times and be well-prepared for the future.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: During business transformation, even with a comprehensive plan, the management still needs to have good communications with their staff, especially when it involves adjustments to work processes or the introduction of automation equipment.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Some staff are accustomed to their current practices and do not want to learn new skills.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Some employees worry that with the company's transformation, they will lose their edge and even fear losing their jobs.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: This kind of mindset is resistant to change.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Looking at the current business environment and advances in new technologies, no one can guarantee that their specialties will always have a market.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, the employers and employees of SMEs and traditional industries must work together to be future-ready.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Here, I would like to suggest a few areas in which the Government can step in to assist on a short-term basis and help the companies continue to transform and remain competitive.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: First, for startups and SMEs, managing startups and ongoing costs is one of the key challenges.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Any schemes that support reduction of their fixed costs will be useful for them to manage their cash flow.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Cost of labour and rental are the main components of their fixed costs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Second, I am glad that Minister Lim Hng Kiang has referred to the fact there would be the LEAD+ programme that would actually provide these shared corporate support functions.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: To take that further, I would suggest that they can also provide job opportunities for some of the retirees who have past management and extensive business experiences.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: A platform can be established for matching these retirees to SMEs and startups to serve as mentors and consultants so that they continue providing their know-how in the field.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Lastly, for businesses, managing cost is only one of the many aspects that they have to handle amidst the challenging economic conditions.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: The silver lining for businesses that survive tough situations is that their businesses would have stress-tested a differentiating edge −.one with an agility to adapt and constantly keep abreast of market trends.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: And the crux of this is the culture within the company and the mindset of the business owners.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: As a step to encouraging more innovation and piloting some of these creative ideas, we need an open, flexible and trusting environment.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: To facilitate this, I hope that the Government could strengthen the framework for IP protection, streamline some of the channels for information search and their applications, as well as to leverage the trade networks that could assist them in future expansion as part of the transformation process.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: Mr Chairman, businesses, in particular SMEs, are being affected by global factors, such as a slowdown in China, as well as domestic factors, such as high business costs.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: During the debate on the President's Address, I spoke on the slowing economy.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: The numbers for this year continue to paint a gloomy picture.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: In the face of these challenges, business confidence among SMEs has been slipping.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: Can MTI share what is the Government doing to help companies ride through this difficult period?

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad
text: Mr Chairman, I regard the ITP which the Minister for Finance has outlined in his Budget speech as highly significant.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad
text: It is a mega shift which Singapore is about to embark on.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad
text: I am quite certain this will have a significant impact and repercussions on our SMEs at all levels.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad
text: I am also quite concerned with those SMEs at the lower segment, especially if a one-size-fits-all approach is taken.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad
text: This is especially so when there are gaps of varying degrees of capabilities and competencies among our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad
text: We can roughly say that there are various types of SMEs: the normal SMEs, small SMEs, very small SMEs and very, very small SMEs, and even further down the road.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad
text: With each facing its own unique difficulties, I am sure each will also need to find its own set of formulas and solutions to survive and grow.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad
text: From financing to resources, to processes and organisational capabilities, each SME has to decide what has to be focused on.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad
text: I reckon this is like a sportsperson who wants to improve on his performance.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad
text: Engaging a coach will then suggest that the sportsperson will undergo a step-by-step regime, thus building up the right muscles to elevate his or her strategic parts of the body and, ultimately, toning up the muscles where they really need for that particular type of sport.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad
text: Not embarking on the right regime may lead to the wrong muscles being developed and, hence, not able to reach the desired outcome.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad
text: I would presume that, likewise, this is needed in the growing of our SMEs from one level to the next, thus moving in tandem with the overall strategic goals of the nation.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad
text: I reckon it is well understood that different regimes have to be offered to the different levels of SMEs.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad
text: My question, henceforth, is: has the Ministry already planned or is in the process of planning a targeted approach for the lower level SMEs which, I presume, will need very specific, if not customised assistance?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: There is also concern that a significant portion of the Budget seems to be tailored towards helping the larger SMEs.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Mr Chairman, I am heartened by the Minister for Finance's emphasis on fostering innovation and improving productivity in the latest Budget.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Targeted support for hiring of older workers, as well as automation efforts, are steps in the right direction as our workforce matures and we face constraints with the number of foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: There are also measures in this Budget that help SMEs to embrace innovation and improve productivity.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: ITP and TechSkills Accelerator are exciting initiatives that help our companies and workers adapt to rapidly changing economic realities.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Tharman has also said on several occasions that our workers need to develop deep skills, in particular, in the finance and logistics sectors.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: He used the term "deep mastery" and referred to the German model of Mittelstand companies.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The Mittelstand companies are the rough equivalent of our SMEs but they are also quite different.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: They are very focused on doing something really well, are very nimble and customer-centric.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But what really differentiates the Mittelstand companies from Singapore SMEs is that they have a very strong system of apprenticeship that helps their workers develop deep skills.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is these deep skills, developed over time and generations, that give Mittelstand and, indeed, German Industry, their competitive edge in the world.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Exceptions to be found are in the traditional professions of medicine, law and accounting where training is still considered very much a part of the apprenticeship process.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is no surprise that these examples are considered highly skilled professions.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: That is not a very encouraging statistic in terms of productivity.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: And I suspect this is due to the fact that our SMEs do not have a robust apprenticeship system that engenders the development of deep skills.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Job-hopping between companies and sectors almost certainly does not lead to deep skills.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Deep skills are needed not just for productivity but for innovation as well.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Innovation is not about sitting around and having a "Eureka" moment.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The beautiful fonts we associate today with Apple computers and iPhones were due to the fact that Steve Jobs attended calligraphy classes in college conducted by a former Trappist Monk called Robert Palladino who had mastery of calligraphy and fonts.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Locally, the salted egg yolk croissant which has become very popular lately is also a result of deep skills.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: If you cannot make a decent croissant, you certainly cannot make a good salted egg version.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: So, I would like to ask the Minister what measures are in place to encourage SMEs to give apprenticeships and what incentives are there to engender the spirit of apprenticeship among our workforce.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Our workers must look at apprenticeship as a necessary step to developing deep skills and, hence, excellence.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Mr Chairman, over the years, we know our average productivity growth has slowed.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: This is especially so for sectors, such as retail and F&B.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Companies in these sectors are also faced with constraints, from a tight labour market to high business costs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Deputy Prime Minister Tharman also highlighted recently that there has been a divergence in productivity growth between outward-oriented sectors and domestically-focused ones.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I note that a number of efforts have been made by various agencies to encourage innovation and the usage of technology to boost productivity, but the impact on productivity has not been evident.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Have we got to the root cause of this issue?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: How have our productivity initiatives been working, in particular, for the domestically-oriented sectors?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Can MTI share the efforts to capture new measures of productivity that can be monitored for policy purposes?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: What is MTI's strategy to raise productivity growth, particularly in the most affected sectors?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: And if we already have one, are we on track?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: It suggests that either wages will eventually have to fall as we price ourselves out of the market, or productivity has to go up.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: But the latter would need some concerted effort and focus, and current measures may need more time before we can see the benefits.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Mr Chairman, in Budget 2016, the Government has pledged more resources to our TACs and it is no doubt good that we aim to level up TACs to play more of a pan-industry role.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: But I would like to sound one cautionary note.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: TACs are, generally, run by an executive committee (exco) that consists of representatives from different companies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: If there is to be much greater involvement in communication with Government agencies, it is the exco and staff reporting to the exco at the TACs who will be on the frontline of that communication.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Those exco members also have their own individual corporate interests.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: In working with TACs, I urge MTI to take pains to ensure that communication efforts and engagement are as inclusive as possible towards all TAC members.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: This is so as to mitigate any risk that the TAC exco members will use or will be perceived, rightly or wrongly, to be using any access to Government resources or information for the benefit of their own firms, rather than for the whole TAC membership.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Promptly circulating minutes of meetings between the Government and the TAC staff and exco to all members would be one way to manage this.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: Chairman, it has been announced in this Budget of the increased role for TACs in helping their respective sectors transform and scale up.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: The pivotal roles that TAs play in supporting their industries have a long history dating back to the Middle Ages.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: Today, in some of the most competitive economies, such as the US and Germany, TAs fulfil wide-ranging functions, including lobbying and guiding Government regulations, setting standards and best practices, R&D, upgrading processes and products in their industry, education and professional development for those employed in their industries and, often, they also act as a watchdog and develop codes of practice to increase stakeholders' confidence.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: In Korea and Taiwan, TACs act as formidable consortiums to capture overseas business.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: In contrast, Sir, SMEs in Singapore tell me that TACs here have much room to step up to the role expected of them.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: With a few exceptions, most TACs have weak capabilities and few resources despite being most sincere about the intentions to support their industries.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: Most companies I spoke to are sceptical of TACs' abilities to lead the development of industry-wide transformation projects.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: But, Sir, the LEAD programme has already been in operation for over 10 years.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: How can TACs start to position themselves for the pivotal role demanded of them in this Budget, which calls for development of transformation roadmaps for over 20 sectors, in order to help companies lift productivity and drive innovation?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: Like the hon Member Mr Thomas Chua, I urge the Government to consider having a larger number of such officers as there is a large number of TACs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: Secondment of public officers will enable the much needed depth of understanding of specific needs of the industries and will empower them to be in a better position to design tailor-made support schemes and specialised infrastructural developments to spearhead transformation and innovation of the industries.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: I hope that all will rise to the challenge and that we will all do our best to support them.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: In 2013, it was reported that a survey conducted by the Institute of Certified Public Accountants of Singapore found over eight-tenths of respondents wanted measures to reduce rental costs as their number one wish-list items for businesses.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Recently, the economy appears to have hit a bad patch.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: SBF, in their position paper for a Vibrant Singapore, mentioned that even with increased supply and slowing demand for rental premises, rents are still a concern for many businesses.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: This likely reflects their experience with higher annual increases over the longer term.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Over the longer term, access to low-rent premises has diminished, following the corporatisation of JTC assets as well as the commercial pricing of Housing and Development Board (HDB) rentals.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Commercial and industrial rentals have risen substantially over the years.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: This may require actions to, first, take a long-term view of reducing business rentals and have JTC pick up, in part, their former approach of building lower-cost industrial and commercial property before many of their many properties were privatised.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Based on indications of strong demand for existing low-cost facilities, like incubators, this will go a long way towards stimulating the startup and SME sector.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: This would be a welcome investment to nurture the SME sector.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: The extent by which HDB commercial rentals should be lowered can be calibrated based on available Budget surpluses and other considerations.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Chairman, I would like to make a cut on potential adjustments to rental prices.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Such a move could accelerate the rental adjustments to a more sustainable long-run equilibrium.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Mr Chairman, may I declare my interestss as President of the Consumers Association of Singapore (CASE).

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Over the past few years, more and more Singaporeans go online to buy goods and services.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And with more transactions, CASE has also seen more complaints.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The major complaints are: (a) failure to honour; and (b) misleading claims by vendors online.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Consumers are sometimes made to tick some boxes and agree to the vendor's standard terms and conditions.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Some of these clauses are unfair or unreasonable.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For example, one vendor made it compulsory for disputes to be referred to arbitration, knowing full well that most disputes involve smaller sums and consumers cannot afford the high costs of arbitration.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It also means the ouster of the jurisdiction of the Small Claims Tribunal.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Make it compulsory for vendors or retailers to provide clearer product information and full details about the online retailers.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Ban the practice of having pre-ticked boxes whereby consumers are misled to agreeing to certain terms unless they know how to untick the boxes.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Ensure that all disputes can still be referred to the Small Claims Tribunal and not restricted to arbitration.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: CASE is also concerned that more and more businesses are collecting prepayment for their products.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: When the business fails, consumers would not be able to recover their deposits and would suffer losses.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I urge the Ministry to consider introducing laws to ensure that prepayment deposits collected are paid to an escrow account only and not directly to the business or, alternatively, some other ways to protect prepayment deposits for consumers.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This will allow consumers to know which is the cheapest petrol being sold by the petrol companies and allow greater competition.

speaker: The Chairman
text: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mr Chairman, may I have your permission to display some slides later on in my speech?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As mentioned by the Minister for Trade Lim Hng Kiang, we recognise that companies are facing headwinds this year.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Some sectors will be more affected than others.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Yee Chia Hsing and Miss Cheryl Chan asked about how the Government will help SMEs ride through this period.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: During this year's Budget Statement, the Minister for Finance announced a number of measures to address the near-term concerns of our companies, especially SMEs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And these include measures, such as the enhanced corporate income tax rebate, holding off foreign worker levies for certain selected sectors and the new SME Working Capital Loan Scheme.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: EDF 5 will support existing SPRING and IE Singapore schemes, and EDF 5 will go towards supporting ITP that the Minister for Finance has announced.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa may wish to note that this will go towards supporting SMEs to upgrade and capture new growth opportunities.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But even as we set aside more funds for development of local enterprises, we are also sharpening our assistance schemes to make sure that our interventions are more targeted.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This will ensure that we get the most out of our limited resources.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For instance, we will put more resources into schemes that have created the biggest impact on our SMEs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I am glad to also announce that another scheme will be enhanced which is the Ministry of Communications and Information (MCI) and IDA's Infocomm for Productivity and Growth (IPG), which is funded from the National Productivity Fund (NPF).

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And to maximise impact, we will also support the costs of solutions across all branches of the business.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Depending on their specific needs, many SMEs have made use of the $5,000 Innovation and Capability Voucher (ICV) for consultancy services, and to adopt the various Integrated Solutions, such as fleet management systems and mobile ordering and payment schemes.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, there are solutions that SMEs can adopt based on their individual specific needs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But the key challenge is in the outreach to this diverse group of 116,000 local micro-enterprises which can range from our HDB heartlander shops to a car workshop, for example.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: To make Government assistance more accessible to SMEs, especially the smaller ones, SPRING has worked with TACs to set up a network of 12 SME Centres, all across Singapore, housed within TACs, our Community Development Council (CDC) offices as well as within the heartlands.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Like general practitioner (GP) clinics, these SME Centres have been serving as the first port of call for SMEs and providing one-to-one consultations on business and productivity assistance.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But I hope that SMEs will also take the opportunity to be proactive in seeking help from these SME Centres, especially if they are in need of assistance.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As mentioned by the Minister for Finance, the second half of 2016 will also see the public launch of the Business Grants Portal, which will make grants even more accessible to our SMEs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Ms Sun Xueling shared her concerns about SMEs' access to information.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Apart from one-to-one consultations at these 12 SME Centres, our economic agencies like SPRING and IE Singapore have been conducting regular dialogue sessions with SMEs to discuss the latest trends and opportunities for SMEs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Just last week, SME Centres held a Convention for SMEs to share knowledge on business model transformation and innovation.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Additionally, SMEs can also visit SPRING's SME Portal, which is in both English and Chinese-language, for information on broad level industry trends, business guides as well as business opportunities.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Our companies, especially in the SME sector, must transform and do so urgently.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As a small country with limited resources, we cannot compete on costs alone.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We recognise that costs, as Miss Cheryl Chan pointed out, continue to be of concern to businesses.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The two business costs often cited by businesses are labour and rent, as Mr Chen Show Mao said earlier.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The truth about labour costs is that between 2009 and 2015, real wage growth outpaced productivity growth.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: While labour productivity, as measured by value-added per worker, rose by 2.2% per annum over this period, the real median income of full-time employed residents, however, rose by a higher 2.5% per annum.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This has contributed to an increase in unit labour cost of 1.5% per annum over the same period.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Therefore, we need to press on with increasing our productivity to keep pace with wage increases.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Chen Show Mao expressed concerns about rental costs in our shops.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Henry Kwek also suggested that steps be taken to lower rents should the economic situation worsen.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But in reality, rents are already coming down and will continue to face downward pressure from a further supply of rental spaces coming on stream.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In 2015, industrial rents fell by 2.1% compared to the previous year.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked about the root cause of our slow productivity growth.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Productivity growth in the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development economies, for example, has fallen below 1% since 2012 and has remained weak at 0.3% in 2014.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: More than five years into our national productivity drive, we are on track to achieve the Economic Strategies Committee's target of 2% to 3% productivity growth for the decade as a whole from 2009 to 2019.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: However, most of this was due to the high productivity growth in 2010.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: At the sectoral level, however, the situation is somewhat more varied.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Some sectors, especially the outward-oriented ones, are doing better than others.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For example, since 2009, our finance and insurance sector achieved productivity growth of 4.7% per annum.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: On the other hand, our domestic sectors, such as retail and food services, where the bulk of the companies are still heavily reliant on manpower, are not doing as well.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Therefore, we need to press on with productivity drives in these weaker sectors.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked about our productivity strategies going forward.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For our productivity drive to succeed, we must go beyond Government incentives and Government measures.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Under the second five-year Retail Productivity Plan that was announced last year, one key focus area is sales growth.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: SPRING will support retailers to improve their online sales by collaborating with e-commerce players, such as SingPost, Google, eBay and RedMart.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This will be especially helpful for retailers who already have their own brands as they can reach out to markets beyond Singapore.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: According to a recent report by Bain and Company, two-thirds of the 150 million digital consumers in Southeast Asia are already shopping online.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is a huge online market compared to the physical market of five million in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: A number of local retailers understand that the opportunity for e-commerce is here and now.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Forward-looking businesses are already changing in response to the changing consumer shopping habits.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Singapore Food Manufacturers' Association (SFMA) has also worked with IE Singapore to launch the first Singapore Pavilion e-commerce shopfront on Tmall.com, China's largest e-commerce marketplace.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We have been focusing a lot on what the Government should do and how our businesses can transform.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: However, the reality is that businesses also respond to consumer needs and behaviour, and the retail sector cannot transform quickly enough if consumer mindsets and purchasing habits do not change.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Consumers can also play their part in helping our businesses to transform.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For example, we have been working with the major supermarkets to proliferate the use of "self-checkout counters".

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: If consumers adopt such behaviours, it will help to release manpower from these supermarkets to do higher value jobs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: To shift consumer mindsets, MTI has launched a series of publicity campaigns to promote this "Do-it-yourself (DIY) culture" within our consumers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In a survey conducted after the campaigns, 94% of respondents said they were aware of such self-checkout facilities.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Among these, 97% of them have used the facilities.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: If consumers play their part and we see businesses responding to it, we will get better traction in our productivity drive.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Thomas Chua asked about the need to help our traditional sectors transform and upgrade.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: One key strategy is the cluster development approach to revitalise and transform traditional sectors.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We want to create a social environment where co-located SMEs can collaborate more with one another and find common solutions to solve common problems.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Miss Cheryl Chan may wish to note that by clustering companies from sector-specific areas together, SMEs can share infrastructure and services to enjoy better economies of scale and lower the start-up costs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: With reference to Mr Chen Show Mao's comment, this is one way that we have changed how we use business space while maintaining affordability and competitiveness.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For example, the JTC Food Hub@Senoko, conceptualised jointly by JTC, SFMA and the Singapore Manufacturing Federation (SMF), houses a shared cold room and warehouse facility (CWF).

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: At the food hub signing ceremony I attended last week, food manufacturing and services companies told me that they could save on start-up and operating costs by tapping on these ready-built facilities and services offered by the CWF operator.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: To be completed in 2020, this multi-storey MMT Hub will have high ceilings and heavy floor loading to accommodate tenants' heavy automation machinery and products.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: These specifications will then allow companies to explore productive initiatives, such as the installation of overhead cranes, to replace and reduce their reliance on fork lifts.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Beyond our local environment, SMEs must also pay attention to the global environment and seize opportunities as they arise.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As Mr Liang Eng Hwa pointed out, the Market Readiness Assistance (MRA) programme and Global Company Partnership (GCP) programme were enhanced last year to help companies internationalise and take advantage of these overseas business opportunities.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And under the GCP programme, over 3,800 companies received help to grow their business overseas in 2015.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: IE Singapore introduced a new tax incentive – the International Growth Scheme, and expanded the scope of Internationalisation Finance Scheme to include mergers and acquisitions.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Thirdly, we introduced more targeted assistance to address the manpower needs of internationalising companies.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: IE Singapore enhanced the Double Tax Deduction for Internationalisation (DTDi) to include qualifying manpower expenses for Singaporeans who are posted overseas.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This supports businesses that are expanding overseas and creates more skilled jobs and opportunities for our Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Minister for Finance has announced that the scheme will be extended for another four years until 31 March 2020.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Minister for Industry, Mr S Iswaran, talked about the ITP.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: One key plank of this effort is our partnership with our TAs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Chairman, if I may now speak in Mandarin.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: (In Mandarin):   Ms Foo Mee Har and Mr Thomas Chua spoke about the role of our TACs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: With over 300 TACs in Singapore, the TAC landscape is very diverse – ranging from the broad-based ethnic chambers, to industry associations, as well as smaller TACs with only a handful of members.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Government has been working closely with the business-focused TACs to reach out to SMEs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For instance, our apex chamber, the SBF, is one of our key partners in the Committee on the Future Economy (CFE).

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Besides working together with the broad-based TACs, our economic agencies will need to take a more targeted approach to drive transformation of our key sectors.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For ITP to be implemented successfully, effective partnerships with TACs are crucial.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: If SME Centres can be compared to GP clinics, then the role of TACs in ITP would be akin to that of "specialist doctors".

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: First, businesses best understand the trends, opportunities and challenges of their sectors.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In this regard, TACs can play a critical role in leading the transformation of their respective sectors, by organising the industry players and set the direction for growth and transformation of the sector.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Government has to work hand in hand with our businesses.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: There is a saying that "the business arena is like the battlefield"; businesses should work closely with one another to achieve greater results.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In this regard, the Government can set the economic strategies but, at the tactical level, businesses must still lead the charge.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Second, TACs' extensive reach and business networks also create a multiplier effect for the Government to touch base with many more SMEs than Government agencies alone are able to.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Ms Sun Xueling had asked about how SMEs can be alerted to business trends and opportunities.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Leon Perera may also wish to note that Government support for TACs is carefully scoped out and meant to create as wide an impact as possible.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Since 2005, SPRING and IE Singapore have worked with 35 TACs on various sector upgrading projects under the LEAD programme.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Third, TACs can also support their sectors' growth by facilitating the aggregation of demand and provide shared resources for the industry.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This can free up the time and energies of many SMEs and allow them to focus on their core functions.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Fourth, TACs can embark on Operation and Technology Roadmapping (OTR) with A*STAR under the GET-Up Programme for their respective sectors.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: OTR is a detailed step-by-step plan that lays out the technological capabilities needed for companies or sectors to remain competitive.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Fifth, as Mr Thomas Chua has noted, TACs can also bring SMEs together and help them internationalise.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For example, a number of TACs have worked with IE Singapore on the Deal Hunter Programme to help SMEs source for business leads on a collective basis.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For TACs that are willing and ready to take on a larger role, the Government will put in more resources to build up their capabilities.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Ms Foo Mee Har and Mr Thomas Chua may wish to note that we will be introducing the LEAD+ programme to help TACs from selected sectors.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For a start, we will be working more closely with TACs that have already achieved a certain level of competency, and from priority sectors for transformation and growth.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: To help address the need for leadership development among TACs, SPRING's LEAD+ programme will support selected TACs on strategic planning, succession planning within TACs, as well as groom younger leaders.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In addition, SPRING will also support the upgrading of internal processes within TACs, such as in HR, information technology and finance, by providing funding for consultancy, hardware and software upgrading.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: To spur transformation of the sector, SPRING will work with TACs under LEAD+ to strengthen the services they provide to their members.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For instance, it will support a wide range of TAC-led activities, including collaboration with Centres of Innovation (COIs), OTR and market sensing activities.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: LEAD+ will be introduced in phases, starting with TACs that are already on board the LEAD programme.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For smaller TACs that may lack the scale or capabilities, I encourage them to start by embarking on LEAD projects with SPRING.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As mentioned by the Minister for Trade Lim Hng Kiang, TACs can also work with SPRING on TAC-Collaborative Industry Projects, in order to benefit their members.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Through these projects, TACs and SMEs can work with our research institutes and tap on new technologies, which could include data analytics and food packaging technologies, as mentioned by Ms Sun Xueling.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For instance, our TACs in the logistics sector can also work with TACs in the food or retail sectors, to provide solutions to one another's problems in a synergistic and complementary manner.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Smaller TACs can also consider moving to the TA Hub at Jurong Town Hall.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: By clustering at the TA Hub, smaller TACs can share facilities, tap on secretariat support from the larger TACs and explore collaboration in areas, such as training and organising overseas missions.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Minister for Finance also spoke widely about the importance of partnerships in the ITP.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But just as importantly, transformation must, first, come from the companies themselves.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We have grants for companies, and TACs can take a proactive role in transformation and innovation.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But all these will come to nought if companies do not have the hunger to transform.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As Mr Thomas Chua mentioned during the Budget debate, SMEs need to have the correct mindset and must want to transform.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: By working with TACs, we want to foster a stronger spirit of self-reliance within our local enterprises.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: (In English): Mr Lim Biow Chuan has asked if more protection for consumers can be legislated.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The  CPFTA is regularly reviewed to ensure that it continues to provide consumers with adequate protection.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We started our review last year and have engaged industry, including CASE, for their views.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We are nearing the end of this review and intend to start public consultations soon.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Those who engage in criminal activities, such as outright cheating, will continue to be investigated by the Police under the Penal Code.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Most CaseTrust-accredited retailers provide protection for consumer prepayments.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We encourage more TAs to work with CASE on accreditation schemes to better safeguard consumers' interests.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Thirdly, the CPFTA provides the same protection to consumers, whether their purchases are made online or from our regular brick-and-mortar retailers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: On practices, such as pre-ticked boxes and arbitration clauses, the CPFTA already requires retailers to make material information clear to consumers prior to these transactions.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We are working with CASE to educate consumers on the importance of reading the terms and conditions before finalising the transaction.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Fourthly, MTI has engaged CASE on making information on petrol prices and discounts more accessible to consumers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: CASE is working towards putting such information on their website.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Chairman, in conclusion, economic restructuring is a long-term effort which cannot be put on hold.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: SMEs must make use of every opportunity to upgrade their capabilities.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Government, too, needs to work closely with the industry on this and, hence, needs to strengthen our partnership with  TACs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I am confident that we will emerge from our challenges a stronger economy, with our SMEs more competitive than before.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Mr Chairman, I would like to thank Members for their comments and suggestions.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The Minister for Trade Mr Lim Hng Kiang, the Minister for Industry Mr S Iswaran and the Minister of State Dr Koh Poh Koon, have explained how our economic strategies will prepare us for the future and create good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: I will now round up MTI's speeches by elaborating on the initiatives specific to renewable energy and manpower that will position Singapore for the future.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Mr Louis Ng asked about the steps we are taking to achieve our renewable energy goals.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Given our geography, solar energy is the most viable form of renewable energy in Singapore.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The Government is, therefore, proactively facilitating the greater deployment of solar energy while ensuring grid stability.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: For example, the Government is funding R&D to facilitate the deployment of solar energy and has streamlined regulations for households using solar power.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The SolarNova programme will play a key role in furthering our plans to raise solar energy deployment in our system.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: To make this happen, we need everyone to be part of this movement − companies, unions, TACs and all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Together, we equip ourselves to stay competitive and relevant.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We need to attune ourselves to new work trends emerging from disruptive technologies and global developments.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Like what the two Ministers have highlighted, there are now jobs in exciting new areas, such as fintech, that did not even exist just a few years ago.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This has led to new job opportunities in fields like data analytics and e-commerce.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: These fast-moving developments are changing the way we work.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Across various sectors, jobs are being optimised through technology solutions.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: As Mr Liang Eng Hwa rightly said, we should gear ourselves to ride the waves of change and seize the opportunities of the future economy.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Mr Chairman, may I have your permission to display some slides on the LED screens, please?

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Take the example of Ms Lilian Yeo, a 58-year-old sales supervisor for Decks.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Decks is the retailer for Surfers Paradise and Island Shop products.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Decks has adopted radio frequency identification (RFID) for both its front- and back-of-house operations.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Lilian's can-do spirit helped her adapt and learn this new technology.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: She is now adept at using RFID and appreciates how technology has eased her job and given her more time to focus on frontline duties like serving and interacting with customers.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: So, like Ms Lilian Yeo, we need to be flexible and stand ready to be trained to develop industry-relevant skills.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: To stay ahead of the curve, we must continue to train and produce workers with skills that meet the demands of industries.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We can open the doors to a better future by embracing the spirit of lifelong learning.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Please allow me to give the House a quick update on the various SkillsFuture initiatives that support Singaporeans on this constant journey, starting with our youths, then the working adults and then  businesses.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We fully agree with Mr Sitoh Yih Pin that one of the ways to engender the development of deep skills is through apprenticeships, particularly for our SMEs.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This not only helps companies to attract talent; it also allows participants to develop deep industry-relevant skillsets during their apprenticeships.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Besides apprenticeships for our youths, we must also nurture in them a curiosity and desire for global exposure.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This can certainly support our companies' internationalisation drive as we grow the pool of talents in our workforce ready with the necessary skillsets to support our external economy.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The ability to work in international teams and harness cross-cultural capabilities are some of the skills that are offered in the Young Talent Programme (YTP) by IE Singapore.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: To prepare them for global careers, YTP offers our students opportunities for overseas immersion through internships and work-study programmes.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I am pleased to report that we will implement the programme in ITEs later this year as well.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This will provide more opportunities for our students to gain international exposure.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Our young people will learn how to navigate across cultures and differences.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This picture shows Mr Raiyan Muhammad bin Musa from Ngee Ann Polytechnic with some of the friends that he met during his internship at The Ascott Limited in Vietnam.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Besides these friends, Raiyan shared with us that he had colleagues from France, the UK, India and Malaysia.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: During the internship, Raiyan learnt how to connect across cultures and nationalities in the workplace.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Such experiences during the formative years will give our young people a potential head start into a global career.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: In addition to building young talent for global jobs, we are also grooming promising Singaporeans to take on leadership positions through the SkillsFuture Leadership Development Initiative (LDI).

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: It aims to grow a pipeline of Singaporean leaders across all career levels.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: As part of LDI, EDB has been partnering companies to design and implement leadership development roadmaps tailored to their business objectives and HR priorities.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: For example, MasterCard's Management Associate Programme has an overseas stint in emerging markets that provides fresh graduates with global exposure and in-market experience across key business units.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Upon completion of the programme, the management associates will be better positioned to take on larger roles in the company.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We all know talent is key for businesses, big or small, to grow and succeed.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: For SMEs that may not have the resources to build up their talent development and worker competencies, we have created the SkillsFuture Mentors Programme under SPRING Singapore.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The agency works with industry partners to build a pool of mentors who support the development of SMEs' capabilities and help them participate in SkillsFuture initiatives.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Over the next three years, we aim to build up a pool of 400 mentors to support 2,000 SMEs across different sectors.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Moving forward, the Government will continue to invest in SkillsFuture to ensure that our workers and companies are well-positioned to meet the challenges of the future.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Mr Chairman, please allow me to continue in Mandarin.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: (In Mandarin):   Upskilling is key to the vitality of our economy.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: It is not only a means to future-proof our workers, but also a key facet of industry transformation.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: As the Minister for Finance and Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) have explained, ITP will integrate our restructuring efforts in productivity, innovation and manpower development at the sectoral level to maximise impact.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: An integral element of this plan is the Sectoral Manpower Plans (SMPs), which identify the strategies and action plans required for developing sector-specific skills.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Last year, SMPs were launched in sectors, such as hotel and retail, setting out five-year manpower strategies that support the growth of these sectors.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: SMPs are developed and implemented together with Sectoral Tripartite Committees (STCs), consisting of unions, TACs and companies.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Through consultations and discussions with various partners, SkillsFuture aims to strengthen the nexus between the needs of industries and manpower development.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: There are also many other ways that our companies can be part of the SkillsFuture movement.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Besides providing training opportunities, our companies can also offer competency-based career progression pathways to motivate and retain talent.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Tee Hai told us that they believe that people are their most important asset and that all their staff are given equal opportunities to upgrade their skills and knowledge.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Mr Kelvin Ong joined the company in 2010.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: He started out not knowing much about logistics.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: But Tee Hai recognised his good performance and potential and sponsored him to study a part-time Diploma in Logistics Management.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I am heartened to learn that, after starting out as a storekeeper, Kelvin is now a logistics supervisor at the company.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Indeed, Kelvin's success is not just his own, but also the company's.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Here, MTI would like to encourage our companies to be long-sighted as well as courageous to innovate and transform, so that they will be well-placed to compete on the international stage.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Besides using technology to improve efficiency, companies must be willing to redesign jobs, train their staff and help them upskill.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: In time to come, with increased productivity, their revenues will also increase.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: From the employees' point of view, the opportunity to take on higher-skilled and higher-value jobs will mean greater job satisfaction and better wages.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Companies that invest in their employees' training and development will be well-positioned to take on the new challenges of our new economy.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We would like to see more companies like Tee Hai Chem who invest in their employees for the future.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: (In English): We understand skills upgrading takes effort and may not be easy for all, especially for mature workers.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: But successful upskilling is possible at any age when one is armed with a positive and can-do attitude.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Take Mr Mohammad Romzi Bin Kassim, for instance.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Romzi's proactive approach towards learning certainly exemplifies SkillsFuture's spirit of passion for lifelong learning.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Mr Chairperson, the Government remains committed to supporting the development of our workforce.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Lilian, Raiyan, Kelvin and Romzi have shown us that all of us can take ownership of our own training and career paths.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We call upon our partners and every Singaporean to come on board the SkillsFuture movement.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Together, we will build a future-ready workforce empowered to overcome challenges and stay on track for success in the global economy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: But also, it requires the officers to adopt a new approach of working beyond just within the service.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: As the Government, you work in a Government agency; but, now, to work with the markets, you work with the businesses.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: So, in terms of resourcing and organising, I would like to ask the Minister how does the Ministry at this stage set up the headcount that is needed, the changes in terms of the different agencies to be able to drive this sector roadmap that was introduced by the Finance Minister?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: What we propose to do is that, in the time-honoured tradition of financial prudence, we will start by working within what we already have.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But, of course, where necessary, and it may well be necessary, we will then seek assistance from the MOF.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Mr Chairman, in his Budget wrap-up speech, the Minister of Finance referred to the Holistic Industry Productivity Scorecard (HIPS) system that is run by SBF, which provides a calculator of productivity and allows companies to log on to the system, input some data, calculate the productivity level and benchmarks the productivity level against certain industry norms.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: If I recall correctly, the Minister for Finance said that there are roughly 80 companies currently using this HIPS system from SBF.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: He said this in response to my suggestion for a national productivity benchmarking system.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, I would like to ask MTI whether they will be working with SBF, perhaps to take this tool and push it out to all the companies that we have.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I believe that we have 180,000 businesses and companies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, that still leaves many, many more companies that have not been using the system.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: If SBF achieves that target, will the Government actually work with SBF to push out this tool, as a benchmarking tool, not just against industry norms and Singapore, but also industry norms globally, so that our SMEs can have a very clear quantifiable view of what they can achieve, what they can aspire to achieve in terms of productivity?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Chairman, I thank the Member for his question.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Government has been working closely with SBF on many initiatives and we will continue to do so.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As far as productivity benchmarking is concerned, there are various benchmarks that can be utilised.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Government publishes labour productivity benchmarks, such as value-added per worker and value-added per actual hour worked.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Government also publishes sector-specific outcome indicators, such as site productivity for the construction sector.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Other than the benchmark that the Member has mentioned, companies can also use the calculator on the "Way to Go" website to determine their productivity and compare it against other benchmarks.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Government's productivity assistance schemes are intended to support all companies and we will continue to utilise benchmarks that are useful for us to assess the productivity of companies.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: With the great initiative to second public officers to TACs to help them deepen their knowledge and to support TACs, I would like to ask the Minister whether the decision-making and empowerment of these officers would be enhanced, so that they can truly do something meaningful, for example, to tailor-make schemes for these sectors?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: Also, if they are empowered, what is the decision-making process so that they can get things through quite quickly, so that the TACs which have got a good plan, can get on with it?

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: The key in seconding public officers to TACs is to strengthen their secretariat because we recognise the key to a successful implementation requires the secretariat to be reinforced.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
